The answer to Wordle #2617 on May 23, 2026 is CHUCK. I burned two guesses on this one because I kept wanting to put an S somewhere. The double C in positions 2 and 3 isn't rare exactly—think "accent" or "accept"—but it still feels like a trap when you're hunting for vowels. Why This Word Fits Today's Puzzle

CHUCK fits the harder end of Bennett's editing style. She likes words that feel common in speech but look weird on paper. The U is buried between two hard consonants, so your typical vowel-first strategy doesn't help much. I usually start with ADIEU or AUDIO, and neither gave me anything useful today. The double C also means you might burn a guess testing single-C words like CLACK or CHECK before you commit to the pair. I saw someone on Twitter mention they got it in two because they went with CRANE then CHUCK. That's either incredible luck or they know something I don't.

Meaning and Everyday Use

CHUCK means to throw something, often without much care. "Chuck me the remote." "Just chuck it in the bin." It's casual, British-leaning English that crossed over into American usage through TV and movies. The word also shows up as a noun—a chuck is the clamp on a lathe that holds your workpiece, and it's the cut of beef between the neck and the rib. I got briefly sidetracked thinking about woodshop class when I should've been solving. The name connection is hard to miss too: Chuck Norris, Chuck Berry, Chuck Palahniuk. If you're ever stuck naming a fictional tough guy, apparently you default to Chuck.

Sounds obvious, but I watched someone miss CHUCK yesterday because they kept trying CLUCK with the L in slot two, forgetting they'd already ruled that out. It means exactly one of A, E, I, O, or U appears in the answer. In CHUCK, that's the U. Sometimes Y acts as a vowel in English, but Wordle doesn't count it as one for hint purposes. This constraint usually makes the puzzle harder because you have fewer anchor points to build around.

More common than most players expect. Words like AGREE, WRECK (if we counted the K, which we don't), and CHUCK show up regularly. I'd estimate 20-25% of answers have some form of repeated letter. If you're not testing for doubles by guess three, you're leaving information on the table.

Medium-hard. It's familiar vocabulary, but the consonant cluster and single vowel trip people up. The double C is the real killer—many solvers don't expect double consonants in short words unless they've been burned before. I'd rate it a 6.5/10 difficulty, harder than VOCAL, easier than something like RHYME.

What should I do if I'm stuck on guess 4 with no vowels found?

Stop hunting vowels and start hunting consonant pairs. Try words with L, R, N, T, S, K, C in combinations you haven't tested. If you haven't tried a U yet, do that—it's the most likely single vowel in a hard puzzle. Our starter words guide has a section specifically for consonant-heavy fallback guesses.

Where in the world is today's answer?

Sierra Leone sits on the southwest coast of West Africa. It is sandwiched between Guinea to the north and east, and Liberia to the southeast. The Atlantic Ocean forms its entire southwestern boundary. The country's shape is defined by a rounded northern border that tapers down to a narrower southern point, creating a profile that looks a bit like a tilted teardrop or a rough oval with a bite taken out of the east side.

Players often confuse it with Liberia because they share similar vegetation colors on map views and both have Atlantic coastlines. However, Liberia is longer and thinner, stretching further south along the coast. Sierra Leone is more compact. If your distance percentage was under 85% but your direction felt off, you likely landed on Guinea or Côte d'Ivoire. The directional arrows in Worldle can lie if you don't account for the map projection. Today's puzzle pointed southeast for many starting guesses from Europe or North America. This makes sense geometrically, but it gets tricky if you guess a country in the wrong hemisphere.

If you guessed a country in South America, say Brazil, the arrow would point northeast. That specific vector eliminates the entire southern half of the globe immediately. Neither fits the curvature. Madagascar is too elongated; Great Britain has a completely different northern profile.
